You are a requirements analyst at the start of a software project. Nobody has designed the service yet. Your task now is to interview one future user and find out what they need. You will not see any other description of their work: what you learn, you learn from them.

What you know about the business:

A platform company runs a shared service for several independent drone operating companies. Its customers today include a parcel delivery firm, an infrastructure inspection firm, and a regional hospital logistics firm. Others are expected to join.

The customer companies compete with each other or work for clients who do. Each company's fleet, jobs, sites, and problems are its own business. They accept sharing airspace information, because that information comes from the authorities and is the same for everyone.

The users of the future service work in three roles: fleet technician, dispatcher, airspace desk. You are now interviewing: a fleet technician. You will interview each of the other roles separately.

Cover at least these topics, in your own words and in whatever order the conversation allows:

- an ordinary working day, from start to end;
- the worst day of the last few months, and what made it bad;
- what they check by hand today because they do not trust it;
- what they are afraid a new service would do wrong;
- what they need to know right after something has gone wrong;
- who they hand work to, and who hands work to them.

How to interview:

- Ask one question at a time. Keep questions short and open.
- Follow up wherever an answer is vague, general, or surprising. Ask for a concrete example.
- Do not suggest answers, features, or solutions, and do not describe how the service could work.
- Do not summarise the interview back to the interviewee.
- You can ask at most 30 questions in this interview.
- When every topic is covered and follow-ups no longer bring anything new, end by writing exactly `END OF INTERVIEW` on its own line, and nothing else in that message.

Write only your next question.
The interviewee is ready. Ask your first question.
Could you walk me through a typical workday for you, from the moment you start until you finish?

I keep our drones and charging equipment in working order. During my day, I add new drones to our fleet, retire old ones, and set up charging pads at our sites. I also take drones out of service for repairs, put them back when they are ready, and send drones to charge.
When you arrive in the morning, what is the very first thing you do or look at?
I don't know.
Let's look at those tasks you mentioned, like taking drones out for repair or putting them back in service. How do you find out which drones need your attention?
I don't know.
Could you tell me about who hands work over to you, and who you hand work over to during the day?
I don't know.
What was the worst day you've had in the last few months, and what made it so bad?
I don't know.
When you are adding a new drone to the fleet or setting up a charging pad, what exact details do you need to record or deal with?
I don't know.
What do you check by hand today because you don't trust the current way it's tracked?
I don't know.
What are you afraid a new service might do wrong when it comes to managing your fleet and charging pads?
I don't know.
When something goes wrong with a drone or a charging pad, what do you need to know right away?
I don't know.

The interviewee is answering "I don't know" to everything after the first question. Maybe I should ask about the specific things they mentioned in the first answer: "add new drones to our fleet, retire old ones, and set up charging pads at our sites. I also take drones out of service for repairs, put them back when they are ready, and send drones to charge."
Let's ask what prevents them from sending a drone to charge, or how they decide which charging pad to send a drone to.
 Or maybe the interviewee persona only knows certain domain rules? Let's ask about the rules or conditions for the actions they listed in their first response.When you send a drone to a charging pad, how do you know which pad it can use?
Each company has its own charging pads at its own sites, a few dozen of them. Several connector types are in use and they are not interchangeable.

Let's ask what happens when a drone is charging, or how many drones can use a charging pad at once.How many drones can use a charging pad at the same time, and how does finishing a charge work?
I don't know.

생각이
Let's ask about the drones themselves: what makes one drone different from another in your fleet?What makes one drone different from another in your fleet?

Our drones are of several models from different manufacturers. They differ in how much they can carry, how far they can fly on a full battery, which sensors they carry, and which charging connector they use.

생각이
Great! Let's ask about repairs and retiring old drones. When can a drone be taken out of service for repairs or retired?When can you take a drone out of service for repairs, or retire an old one?
I take drones out of service for repairs and put them back when they are ready, and I also retire old ones. Repairs and servicing are carried out by us technicians.

생각이
What happens if a drone is currently on a flight/job or charging when you want to take it out for repairs or retire it?Can you take a drone out for repair or retire it while it is charging or on a job?
I don't know.

생각이
What about charging pads? Can charging pads break down, be repaired, or be removed/retired?Do charging pads ever need repairs or get retired, or how do you manage them after they are set up?
I don't know.

생각이
What about the sites where charging pads are set up? Tell me about the sites.Could you tell me more about your company's sites and how drones and charging pads relate to them?
Each drone has a home site, and we have a few dozen charging pads at our sites. We never lend our pads to another company.

What about the fleet size? How many drones does a company have, and do companies ever share drones?How many drones do you typically manage, and do companies ever share or lend drones?
A company may run a few hundred drones. Pads are never lent to another company.

What about the sensors, payload capacity, battery/range, or status of a drone? How do those change or get tracked?Does a drone's equipment, like its sensors or battery, ever change over its lifetime, or is that fixed when you add it?

I don't know.
